abstentions: Whether the surface language grammar permits a binder or let-bound name to shadow a component state or const name (determines whether claims 1 and 2 triggers are reachable or latent)
Whether the intended scoping semantics is local-binding-wins for shadowed names (determines the correct behavior and whether the observed qualification split is a defect or an intentional rule)

findings.description: rewrite_lvalue (687-698) routes LValue::Var and LValue::Index names through rewrite_state_name (700-706), which prefixes any name in component.names.state without consulting bound; bound is applied only to the Index sub-expression via rewrite_expr, never to the variable name itself. This is asymmetric with rewrite_statement's ForAll arm (670-683), which clones bound and inserts the binder before rewriting the body, and with rewrite_expr's Var arm (711-717), which guards qualification on !bound.contains(&name). Effect: within a ForAll (or Quantified/Aggregate) body whose binder name matches a component state name, an assignment or index target to that name is still prefixed to alias.x by rewrite_state_name while the identical name in the rvalue is left bare by rewrite_expr, producing alias.x := f(x) instead of the intended x := f(x). Reachability caveat: whether the surface grammar permits a binder to shadow a component state name is not established in the available projections; if shadowing is illegal, this asymmetry is latent rather than triggerable. The downstream kernel behavior for the mixed qualification is not in the projections, so the kernel-corruption consequence is inferred from the immediate qualification split rather than observed.
findings.title: Lvalue rewrite ignores the bound set, creating asymmetric qualification between lvalue and rvalue for shadowed names

findings.description: rewrite_action_items (609-631) processes each ActionItem independently via .map with the same immutable bound reference; the Let arm (623-625) rewrites only the initializer expression and never inserts the bound name into bound. This contrasts with rewrite_binder (844-855), Expr::Quantified (796-802), and Expr::Aggregate (810-816), which all clone bound and insert the binder name before rewriting the body. The .map structure makes per-item bound extension impossible without restructuring the function, and Let is an ActionItem rather than a Statement, so there is no other path that would add its name to bound. Effect: if a let-bound name matches a component state or const name, a subsequent item's rvalue reference to that name is still rewritten by rewrite_expr's Var arm (711-717) to alias.name (the state/const) because !bound.contains(&name) still holds, rather than resolving to the local binding. Reachability and intent caveats: whether the surface grammar permits a let name to shadow a state/const name is not established in the projections; whether the intended scoping semantics is local-binding-wins is an interpretation rather than a projected fact; and the encoding of the subsequent reference as Expr::Var is assumed from the description rather than shown in a projection.
findings.title: Let arm in rewrite_action_items does not extend bound, unlike all other binder forms

findings.description: rewrite_expr ends in `other => other` (840) and rewrite_type ends in `other => other` (589): any Expr/TypeExpr variant not explicitly enumerated is returned unchanged, with no qualification of embedded identifiers and no compile-time exhaustiveness error. Trigger: any fall-through variant carrying unqualified state/const/type names (including variants added later) yields unresolvable references in the lowered kernel; the catch-all makes the omission silent. Expr::Call likewise leaves its name unqualified (742-749), which is sound only if call names are always global.
findings.title: Non-exhaustive rewrite_expr/rewrite_type catch-alls (other => other) silently pass unhandled variants through without qualification

summary: Three findings in compose.rs name-qualification rewrite. Two are real structural asymmetries in how bound is threaded — the lvalue path ignores bound for names while the rvalue path honors it, and the Let arm never extends bound unlike all other binder forms; both are confirmed in source but their triggers depend on shadowing legality that is absent from the projections. The third (non-exhaustive catch-all arms) is a confirmed latent hazard, properly hedged. All three share the same projection gap: AST enum definitions, surface-language binding rules, and downstream kernel semantics are unavailable, so trigger-reachability and consequence claims are inferred rather than observed.
